question.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0, \\ L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

find $L\{u(t-6)\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\pi t)\},$ where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.
question.worked_solution:
The second shifting theorem states that if $a\ge 0$ and $L\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\}$ exists for $s>{s}_{0},$ then

$$
L\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\}={e}^{-as}\,L\{g(t+a)\},\,\text{for}\,s>{s}_{0},
$$

where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.

In our case, we wish to find

$$
L\{u(t-6)\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\pi t)\}.
$$

Therefore, $a=6,$ and we have 

$$
L\{u(t-6)\,g(t)\}={e}^{-6s}\,L\{g(t+6)\},
$$

where $g(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\pi t).$

Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}g(t+6) & =sin\,(7\pi (t+6)) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\pi t+42\pi ) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡7\pi t\operatorname{cos}⁡42\pi +\operatorname{cos}⁡7\pi t\operatorname{sin}⁡42\pi  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡7\pi t\cdot 1+\operatorname{cos}⁡7\pi t\cdot 0 \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡7\pi t.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)\}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}$ for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{g(t+6)\} & =L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\pi t)\} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{{s}^{2}+49{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the second shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{u(t-6)\,g(t)\} & ={e}^{-6s}\,L\{g(t+6)\} \\  & ={e}^{-6s}\cdot \frac{7\pi }{{s}^{2}+49{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$
